editorial.headline: Building the Places Where Sport Happens
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 42994 covers the construction, upkeep and rebuilding of sports facilities, from stadiums and pools to golf courses and athletic tracks.
editorial.body:
KBLI 42994 is the construction activity behind the physical settings of sport. Its scope reaches beyond a stadium build: it includes constructing, maintaining and rebuilding facilities such as football, baseball and rugby grounds; motor-racing tracks; basketball, hockey and tennis courts; golf courses; swimming pools; athletics tracks; archery ranges and indoor sporting arenas. The code therefore speaks to the built infrastructure that allows competition, training and public sport to take place.

The activity is open to businesses at large, micro, small and medium scales. That breadth matters because the scope can accommodate both major facility works and the continuing maintenance or redevelopment of existing sporting assets. The classification also records the relevant civil-construction subclassifications as ST009 and BS016, placing the work firmly in the specialist world of sports-facility construction rather than in the operation of sport itself.

Nationally, the PMA position is straightforward: the activity is open, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. Put differently, the national record allows full foreign ownership for this activity. The governing reference listed for that position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Nothing in the record adds a separate national ownership condition, so the editorial fact is simply the stated ceiling.

Bali calls for a more precise reading, without any cause for pessimism. This activity is not blocked by the provincial moratorium recorded here. Bali’s rule blocks PMA for all low- and medium-low-risk KBLI activities across the province on a permanent basis; however, for this activity the OSS risk at the large scale is medium-high or high. That is why the record gives Bali the status `OK_or_HIGHER_RISK` and states that it is not blocked by the moratorium. For a foreign-owned construction business considering sports-facility work in Bali, the material distinction is clear: the activity remains open nationally at up to 100% foreign ownership, and Bali’s stated moratorium does not bar it on the recorded risk basis.
